title: Unsafe Is a Contract
goal: The unsafe keyword does not turn checks off. It signs a responsibility.

sections.text: An `unsafe` block does not disable the borrow checker or any other rule you have learned. It unlocks a small set of extra operations, like dereferencing raw pointers and calling `unsafe` functions. For those operations the compiler cannot verify the safety conditions, so the block is your signature: you have checked them yourself.

sections.caption: The block marks exactly where the manual argument lives.

sections.text: A function whose caller must uphold conditions is marked `unsafe fn`, and calling it without an `unsafe` block is error `E0133`. Good practice documents those conditions in a Safety section, and good design keeps the unsafe surface small: a tight `unsafe` block inside a safe function, argued once, invisible to callers. That is how the standard library is built.

The last instinct is knowing when not to use it. Application code rarely needs `unsafe`. Before reaching for a tool like `transmute`, check whether std already provides a safe method; usually it does, like `u32::to_le_bytes` for reading integer bytes. Unsafe you avoided is unsafe you never have to argue for.

explanation: unsafe marks where you verified what the compiler cannot. Keep the surface small, document the contract, and prefer a std method when one exists.
